content: 1. Conjugated synthetic estrogens can reduce the effectiveness or levels of ubrogepant by influencing the metabolism of the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4. Therapy adjustments and close monitoring are recommended when ubrogepant is used alongside moderate or weak CYP3A4 inducers. Refer to dosage modification guidelines for further details. 2. Vancomycin can decrease the levels or effects of conjugated synthetic estrogens by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of the hormone. While the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised. 3. Verapamil can increase the levels or effects of conjugated synthetic estrogens by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism and the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 4. Voriconazole can elevate the levels or effects of conjugated synthetic estrogens by influencing CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 5. Zafirlukast may increase the levels or effects of conjugated synthetic estrogens by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 6. Common side effects of estrogen therapy include abdominal pain, back pain, bloating, breast enlargement or tenderness, headache, nausea, peripheral edema, vomiting, amenorrhea, breakthrough bleeding, corneal curvature changes, depression, diarrhea, melasma, spotting, weight changes, abdominal discomfort or distension, muscle spasms, dizziness, insomnia, breast pain, alopecia, rash, urticaria, and deep vein thrombosis or thrombosis. 7. Estrogen therapy is contraindicated in individuals with documented hypersensitivity, active or historical breast cancer, arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction), thrombophlebitis, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), thrombogenic valvular disease, protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency, or other known thrombophilic disorders. It is also contraindicated in cases of anaphylactic reactions, angioedema, uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes mellitus with vascular involvement, jaundice from prior oral contraceptive use, migraines with aura, estrogen-dependent neoplasia, undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding, liver disease or tumors, and known or suspected pregnancy. 8. Caution is advised in patients with a history of hyperlipidemias, hypertension, hepatic or renal impairment, uterine leiomyomata, porphyria, defects in lipoprotein metabolism, hypertriglyceridemia, ovarian cancer, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and elderly patients. Therapy should also be discontinued four weeks before major surgery or prolonged immobilization. 9. Estrogen therapy should not be used in conditions predisposing to hyperkalemia. Progestins combined with estrogens may pose additional risks compared to estrogen-alone regimens, including adverse effects on lipoprotein metabolism (e.g., lowering HDL, raising LDL) and impaired glucose tolerance. 10. Observational studies have reported an increased risk of breast cancer with estrogen plus progestin therapy and a smaller risk increase with estrogen-alone therapy after several years of use. Risks may persist for over 10 years after discontinuation. The WHI trials also demonstrated increased breast cancer risk with estrogen plus progestin therapy. 11. Use caution in patients with asthma, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, migraines, porphyria, systemic lupus erythematosus, and hepatic hemangiomas, as exacerbations may occur. Estrogen therapy is associated with an increased risk of ovarian and endometrial cancer. 12. Long-term postmenopausal estrogen treatment has been linked to increased risks of myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, DVT/PE, and dementia. Estrogens increase thromboembolic risk in patients on warfarin or oral anticoagulants, potentially necessitating higher anticoagulant doses. 13. Estrogen therapy is not approved for osteoporosis prevention. Exogenous estrogens may exacerbate symptoms of angioedema in women with hereditary angioedema and increase the risk of gallbladder disease. Severe hypercalcemia may occur in women with breast cancer and bone metastases; discontinue therapy and manage serum calcium levels if hypercalcemia develops. 14. Estrogens may cause fluid retention, necessitating monitoring in women with conditions predisposing to fluid retention, such as cardiac or renal impairment. Discontinue therapy if medically concerning fluid retention occurs. 15. Retinal vascular thrombosis may occur; discontinue therapy if sudden partial or complete vision loss, proptosis, diplopia, or migraines develop, pending a visual examination. Permanently discontinue therapy if papilledema or retinal vascular lesions are identified. 16. Consider discontinuing therapy if pancreatitis occurs. Women with pre-existing hypertriglyceridemia may experience elevated plasma triglycerides leading to pancreatitis during estrogen therapy. 17. Monitor thyroid function to maintain free thyroid hormone levels within an acceptable range. Women dependent on thyroid hormone replacement therapy may require increased doses when receiving estrogens. 18. Use caution in women with hypoparathyroidism, as estrogen-induced hypocalcemia may occur. Evaluate whether the benefits of estrogen therapy outweigh the risks. 19. Rare cases of malignant transformation of residual endometrial implants have been reported in women treated with estrogen-alone therapy post-hysterectomy. Consider adding progestin in women with residual endometriosis post-hysterectomy. 20. Estrogen therapy is not indicated during pregnancy. 21. Estrogens are present in human milk and may reduce milk production in breastfeeding women, though this is less likely once breastfeeding is well-established. Consider the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding alongside the mother’s clinical need for therapy and potential adverse effects on the breastfed child. 22. Estrogens are generally acceptable for use, with controlled studies in pregnant women showing no evidence of fetal risk. They replace natural estrogen and are essential for the development and maintenance of the female reproductive system and secondary sexual characteristics. 23. Estrogens are derived from plant sources. Their onset of action for menopause symptoms is typically 2-4 weeks when taken orally. Peak plasma levels occur approximately 8 hours after oral administration. Estrogens are readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, with 80% protein binding. They are metabolized in the liver into inactive sulfates and glucuronides, which are excreted in urine and bile. Metabolites include estradiol, estrone, and estriol. Most estrogens undergo enterohepatic recycling. 24. Adding plans allows for formulary comparisons with other drugs in the same class. Formulary information may vary and change over time. Contact the applicable plan provider for the most current information.
